figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Random CV, block CV, and PPI on one simulated campaign in Vaucluse. Light grey areas are crop parcels. (a) An elevation cutoff draws 1,000 labels, mostly from low-lying parcels. The models make fewer errors there, so random CV (0.903) and 5 km block CV (0.887), which test the models only on these labels, overestimate their performance. (b) A propensity model estimates how likely each parcel was to be labeled. PPI predicts the 5,000 parcels of a deployment sample, then corrects that estimate with the labels, and rarely sampled labels get larger weights. The heavily weighted misclassified labels lower the estimate to 0.775. (c) The crop register labels every parcel, so we know which parcels most of the five fold models misclassify and what their true pooled macro-F1 is (0.769). This is one run of the evaluation stage (Section 2.4).

abstract: Government agencies use crop maps to estimate production, monitor food security, and set agricultural policy. These crop maps are usually validated against field labels, but these labels are rarely a random sample of the area the map covers. Field teams tend to label parcels near roads and skip ones that are small or hard to reach, so performance measured on held-out labels mainly describes the places they visited. We call the difference between this reported performance and performance over the whole mapped region the deployment performance gap. To estimate performance over the whole region, we use a weighted form of prediction-powered inference (PPI). The classifier’s predictions on unlabeled points across the region give a first estimate, and its errors on the labeled points correct that estimate, with more weight on labels from under-sampled conditions. We test this in five European regions where crop registers label every declared parcel, so the true performance is known. Simulating six documented collection practices there produces gaps of up to 0.20 macro-F1. On the collection rule that creates the largest gap in each region, 5 km block cross-validation still overestimates macro-F1 by as much as 0.18, while PPI with weights estimated from satellite embeddings reduces the largest error across regions to 0.07. Importance-weighted cross-validation with the same weights does almost as well, so most of the improvement comes from the weights themselves. We also apply the method to three Kenyan datasets that have no region-wide reference labels. For a roadside dataset collected with helmet-mounted cameras, the estimated macro-F1 falls from 0.93 under random cross-validation to 0.61, although the correction relies on a small number of heavily weighted labels. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/pappi.

sections.body: The introduction argues that crop map evaluations rely on field labels that are rarely a random sample of the mapped region. Enumerators drive along roads and skip small or hard-to-reach parcels, so held-out scores describe only the places visited. The authors call the difference between that score and region-wide performance the deployment performance gap. They propose a weighted form of prediction-powered inference that corrects model predictions with labeled errors, giving more weight to under-sampled conditions. To test it, they simulate six documented collection practices in five regions where true performance is known, then apply the method to Kenyan datasets.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Field labels come from accessible places, so cross-validation on them can overstate crop map performance across the region.

sections.body: The method estimates macro-F1 over a whole deployment region from a labeled sample that is not random. It draws uniform unlabeled deployment points, then starts from the classifier's predicted probabilities across them. A weighted correction is added, equal to the weighted mean of the classifier's errors on labeled points. The weights come from a propensity model, an XGBoost classifier that separates labeled from deployment points, and are inverse odds with propensities clipped to limit extreme values. Intervals use the delta method, and effective sample size shows how concentrated the weights are. Importance-weighted cross-validation with the same weights is a baseline that omits the prediction term. Evaluation uses five regions where crop registers label every parcel, so the true value is known.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Weighted prediction-powered inference estimates region-wide macro-F1 from biased labels, with weights from a propensity model.

sections.body: Random cross-validation overstates deployment macro-F1 by 0.10 or more in at least one region for four collection rules, with the largest gap at +0.198 in Goriška. Block cross-validation removes little of the three largest gaps. On each region's worst-case rule, a weighted estimator leaves the mean error closest to zero among methods usable in practice. Across all six collection rules and five regions, PPI with embedding weights lowers absolute mean error from 0.053 to 0.016, and per-run error from 0.057 to 0.040. Osnabrück's worst-case rule is the exception, where per-run error rises from 0.027 to 0.037. Nominal 95% intervals cover 89% of runs overall and 85% on worst-case rules.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Across all rules and regions, PPI with embedding weights cuts absolute mean error from 0.053 to 0.016.

sections.body: The Kenyan case study applies the method to Helmets, WorldCereal and PlantVillage. None has region-wide reference labels, so the change from random cross-validation is reported instead. In Helmets, each roadside photo yields a crop label and a non-crop label about 20 m apart on the road. Using embedding propensity features and 20,000 deployment points, PPI lowers macro-F1 from 0.93 to 0.61, with a 95% interval of [0.34,0.82]. Block cross-validation gives 0.76. WorldCereal changes by +0.02 and PlantVillage by +0.07. Averaged over 30 runs, the changes are -0.34, -0.08 and +0.05, and only the Helmets change keeps its sign in every run. The effective sample size is 20 of 2,478 labels for Helmets.
sections.heading: Case study: three Kenyan datasets
sections.headline: On the roadside Helmets dataset, weighted correction lowers estimated macro-F1 from 0.93 to 0.61, though it rests on few heavily weighted labels.

sections.body: In the simulations, field-label collection practices create gaps of up to 0.20 macro-F1 between random cross-validation and deployment performance. Block cross-validation and the kNN-distance variant do not consistently remove these gaps, because their evaluation labels still come from the same biased sample. On worst-case rules, PPI with embeddings lowers the largest mean error from 0.18 to 0.07, yet its 95% intervals contain the true value in fewer than 95% of runs. Importance-weighted cross-validation with the same weights is nearly as accurate, and PPI's main advantage is a slightly lower per-run error. The authors recommend reporting PPI estimates with intervals and effective sample sizes beside cross-validation scores. Limitations: the regions were chosen where gaps were likely large, the tests used one binary task and one collection rule at a time, and conditions with few labels make the correction unstable.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: Spatial cross-validation methods do not consistently close the gap, so reporting weighted estimates with intervals is recommended.

sections.body: Tables 4 and 5 list the labels. European regions: Goriška (EuroCrops, 2021, 21,388 parcels, vineyards 26%), Hérault (2018, 27,116, vineyards 83%), Osnabrück (2021, 18,104, silage maize 27%), Vaucluse (2024, 59,241, vineyards 56%), and Bouches-du-Rhône (2024, 23,462, vineyards 27%). Kenyan datasets: Helmets (2,478 labels, crop 50%), WorldCereal (1,720, crop 58%), and PlantVillage (296, maize 67%). Appendix B gives the covariate rescaling and rule shapes, with the floor epsilon set to 0.002 after a sweep in Vaucluse. Appendix C gives the delta-method variance. Appendix D describes the campaign-evaluation input and public covariates. Appendix E reports Helmets land-cover overlap before and after weighting.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the European and Kenyan label summaries, collection-rule formulas, interval derivation, campaign workflow, and Helmets land-cover analysis.
